title: Darkness for idolaters, light for the Word’s followers
source_text: Ἴδωμεν δὲ καὶ τὴν ἑξῆς αὐτοῦ λέξιν, δι᾿ ἧς οἱονεὶ προσωποποιεῖταί τινα, μετὰ τὸ ἀκοῦσαι τούτων τοιαῦτα λέγοντα· πῶς οὖν γνῶ τὸν θεόν; καὶ πῶς τὴν ἐκεῖσε ὁδὸν μάθω; καὶ πῶς αὐτόν μοι δεικνύεις; ὡς νῦν γε σκότον μου τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν προβάλλεις, καὶ οὐδὲν ἐναργὲς βλέπω. εἶτα πρὸς τὸν οὕτως ἐπαπορήσαντα οἱονεὶ ἀποκρίνεται, καί [φησι] τὴν αἰτίαν τοῦ σκότον [εἶναι] τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν κατακεχύσθαι τοῦ εἰπόντος τὰ προειρημένα ἀποδιδόναι νομίζει φάσκων· οὓς ἄν τις εἰς λαμπρὸς φῶς ἐκ σκότους προαγάγῃ, τούτους μὴ δυναμένους ἀντέχειν ταῖς μαρμαρυγαῖς κολάζεσθαι τὴν ὄψιν καὶ βλάπτεσθαι καὶ νομίζειν πηροῦσθαι. καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα δὲ φήσομεν καθῆσθαι μὲν ἐν σκότῳ καὶ ἱδρῦσθαι ἐν αὐτῷ πάντας τοὺς εἰς τὰς τῶν ζωγράφων καὶ πλαστῶν τῶν καὶ ἀνδριαντοποιῶν ἐνορῶντας κακοτεχνίας, μὴ βουλομένους δ᾿ ἀναβλέψαι καὶ ἀναβῆναι τῷ νῷ ἀπὸ ὁρατῶν καὶ πάντων αἰσθητῶν ἐπὶ τὸν ὅλων δημιουργὸν, ὅς ἐστι φῶς· ἐν φωτὶ δὲ τυγχάνειν πάντα τὸν ταῖς τοῦ λόγου αὐγαῖς ἀκολουθήσαντα, δείξαντος ἀφ᾿ ὅσης ἀγνοίας καὶ ἀσεβείας καὶ τῆς περὶ τὸ θεῖον ἀμαθίας ταῦτα ἀντὶ τοῦ θεοῦ προσεκυνεῖτο, καὶ χειραγωγήσαντος τὸν τοῦ βουλομένου σῴζεσθαι νοῦν πρὸς τὸν ἀγένητον καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεόν. „λαὸς“ γὰρ „ὁ καθήμενος ἐν σκοτίᾳ“, ὁ τῶν ἐθνῶν, „φῶς εἶδε μέγα, καὶ τοῖς καθημένοις ἐν χώρᾳ καὶ σκιᾷ θανάτου φῶς ἀνέτειλεν,“ ὁ θεὸς Ἰησοῦς. οὐδεὶς οὖν Χριστιανὸς ἀποκρίνεται τῷ Κέλσῳ ἤ τινι τῶν κατηγορούντων τοῦ θείου λόγου φάσκων· πῶς γνῶ τὸν θεόν; ἕκαστος γὰρ αὐτῶν, ὡς ἐγχωρεῖ, ἔγνω τὸν θεόν. καὶ οὐδείς φησι· πῶς τὴν ἐκεῖσε ὁδὸν μάθω; ἅτε ἀκούσας τοῦ εἰπόντος· „ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια καὶ ἡ ζωὴ“ καὶ γευσάμενος ἐν τῷ ὁδεύειν τῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁδεύειν ὠφελείας. καὶ οὐδεὶς ἂν Χριστιανῶν λέγοι Κέλσῳ· πῶς μοι δεικνύεις τὸν θεόν;
pass_a_gloss: Let us see also his next saying (λέξις), through which he as it were makes a character (προσωποποιέω) of someone, after hearing (ἀκούω) these things, saying such things: 'How then shall I know (γινώσκω) God? and how shall I learn (μανθάνω) the way (ὁδός) there (ἐκεῖσε)? and how do you show (δείκνυμι) him to me? since now you put darkness (σκότος) before (προβάλλω) my eyes, and I see nothing clear (ἐναργής).' Then he as it were answers the one so perplexed (ἐπαπορέω) and thinks to give (ἀποδίδωμι) the cause (αἰτία) of darkness having been poured down (καταχέω) on the eyes of the one who said the foregoing, saying: 'those whom someone leads forth (προάγω) out of darkness into bright (λαμπρός) light (φῶς), these, not able to withstand (ἀντέχω) the gleams (μαρμαρυγή), are punished/afflicted (κολάζω) in sight (ὄψις) and harmed (βλάπτω) and think they are blinded (πηρόω).' To this we will say that sitting (κάθημαι) in darkness and settled (ἱδρύω) in it are all who look into the evil crafts (κακοτεχνία) of painters (ζωγράφος) and modellers (πλάστης) and statue-makers (ἀνδριαντοποιός), not willing to look up (ἀναβλέπω) and go up (ἀναβαίνω) with the mind (νοῦς) from visible (ὁρατός) and all sensible (αἰσθητός) things to the craftsman (δημιουργός) of all, who is light; and that in light is everyone who has followed (ἀκολουθέω) the rays (αὐγή) of the Word (λόγος), [the Word] having shown from how great ignorance (ἄγνοια) and impiety (ἀσέβεια) and unlearning (ἀμαθία) about the divine (τὸ θεῖον) these things were worshipped (προσκυνέω) instead of God, and having led by the hand (χειραγωγέω) the mind of the one wishing to be saved (σῴζω) to the uncreated (ἀγένητος) God over all. For 'the people sitting in darkness' — that of the nations (ἔθνη) — 'saw a great light, and to those sitting in the region (χώρα) and shadow (σκιά) of death light dawned (ἀνατέλλω)' — the God Jesus. No Christian then answers Celsus or any of the accusers (κατηγορέω) of the divine word saying 'How shall I know God?'; for each of them, as is possible (ἐγχωρεῖ), knew God. And no one says 'How shall I learn the way there?', having heard the one who said 'I am the way and the truth and the life', and having tasted (γεύομαι) in journeying (ὁδεύω) the benefit (ὠφέλεια) from journeying. And no Christian would say to Celsus: 'How do you show me God?'
pass_b_english: Let us look also at his next statement, in which he brings on stage, as it were, someone who, after hearing these things, says something like this: “How then am I to know God? And how am I to learn the way there? And how do you show him to me? For now you cast darkness before my eyes, and I see nothing clearly.” Then he gives what is meant as an answer to the one who raised this difficulty, and thinks he is supplying the reason why darkness has been poured over the eyes of the one who said these things. He says: “Those whom someone leads out of darkness into bright light, being unable to bear the brilliance, have their sight afflicted and harmed, and think they have been blinded.”

To this too we shall reply that all those sit in darkness and are settled in it who gaze at the wicked crafts of painters, modellers and makers of statues, and who refuse to look up and to rise in mind from things visible and from everything perceived by the senses to the Maker of the universe, who is light (1 John 1:5). But everyone who has followed the rays of the Word is in light. For the Word has shown from how great an ignorance and impiety, and from how great a want of learning about the divine, these things were worshipped instead of God, and has taken the mind of anyone who wishes to be saved and led it by the hand to the uncreated God who is over all. For “the people who sat in darkness”, the people of the nations, “saw a great light, and for those who sat in the region and shadow of death a light dawned” (Matthew 4:16; Isaiah 9:2), namely Jesus, who is God.

No Christian, then, answers Celsus or any of those who accuse the divine word by saying, “How am I to know God?” For each of them has known God, as far as that is possible. And no one says, “How am I to learn the way there?”, since he has heard the one who said, “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6), and has tasted, in walking it, the benefit that comes from walking it. Nor would any Christian say to Celsus, “How do you show God to me?”

choices.choice: Celsus’s imagined speaker: ‘How then am I to know God? ... I see nothing clearly’; Celsus’s own answer: ‘Those whom someone leads out of darkness into bright light ... think they have been blinded.’ Both are marked as Celsus’s words. The answer clearly draws on Plato’s cave (Republic 515e-516a), but Celsus does not quote it, so no inline citation is given. Bracketed [φησι] and [εἶναι] are Koetschau’s deletions and are not translated. κολάζεσθαι τὴν ὄψιν rendered ‘have their sight afflicted’ (κολάζω here = injure, check, not judicial punishment). The quotation of Isaiah 9:1-2 follows Matthew 4:16 almost word for word (ὁ λαὸς ὁ καθήμενος ἐν σκοτίᾳ ... φῶς ἀνέτειλεν), so Matthew is cited first; Isaiah 9:1 LXX = Isaiah 9:2 in English Bibles. ‘The Maker of the universe, who is light’ is a clear allusion to 1 John 1:5. ὁ θεὸς Ἰησοῦς rendered ‘namely Jesus, who is God’. ἀγένητος (single ν) rendered ‘uncreated’. John 14:6 verbatim. ‘The divine word’ (τοῦ θείου λόγου) here means Christian teaching, so lower-case. ‘I see nothing clearly’ here and ‘I see nothing clearly in your words’ in chapter 67 keep the same English for οὐδὲν ἐναργὲς βλέπω, since Origen turns the phrase back on Celsus.
'those sit in darkness' -> 'all those sit in darkness' (πάντας was left out)

'has led the mind of whoever wishes to be saved by the hand to' -> 'has taken the mind of anyone who wishes to be saved and led it by the hand to' (fixes the stray order that attached 'by the hand' to 'saved')
'a light has dawned' -> 'a light dawned' (aorist ἀνέτειλεν, parallel to 'saw')
